lead: This unit is about meaning: how to write it down, how syntax builds it, and how words and sentences carry it across a discourse. After the unit you can write first-order logic forms, attach meanings to grammar rules, use WordNet and FrameNet, disambiguate word senses, label semantic roles, segment discourse, and resolve pronouns.
about: The unit starts with meaning representation and first-order logic (4.1), the formal language later chapters use. Chapter 4.2 shows how a parser can build those forms rule by rule. Chapter 4.3 turns to the lexicon: word senses and the relations among them. Chapter 4.4 organises those senses into WordNet, FrameNet and multilingual wordnets. Chapter 4.5 uses those resources to choose the right sense in context. Chapter 4.6 moves from words to predicate-argument structure with semantic roles and selectional restrictions. Chapter 4.7 widens the view to discourse: segmentation, coherence and cohesion. Chapter 4.8 closes with coreference and anaphora, where discourse structure and word meaning decide what a pronoun points to.

chapters.idea: A meaning representation is a formal language that lets a computer store a sentence's meaning and draw inferences from it; first-order logic is the standard such language.
chapters.depth: Cover the requirements for a meaning representation: verifiability, unambiguity, canonical form, inferencing, and expressiveness. Introduce first-order logic syntax: constants, variables, functions, predicates, terms, atomic formulae, connectives, quantifiers ∀ and ∃, free and bound variables, scope. Give semantics by model and interpretation: domain, denotation of constants and predicates, satisfaction, entailment. Show restricted quantifiers ∀x(Student(x) → ...) and Davidson's event representation for verbs with an extra event argument. Only a few universities teach description logics; keep that part short: concepts, roles, TBox and ABox, subsumption, one example such as Student ⊑ ∃reads.Book.

figure.aria: Parse tree of the formula for every student reads a book; the existential quantifier sits inside the scope of the universal quantifier.

chapters.example: Represent 'Every student reads a book' in first-order logic. Domain D = {Ravi, Meera, Gita, book1, book2}. Student = {Ravi, Meera}; Book = {book1, book2}; Reads = {(Ravi, book1), (Meera, book2)}. (a) Write the formula. (b) Show that the model satisfies it. (c) Change Reads to {(Ravi, book1)} and say why the formula is false. (d) Explain why ∃y(Book(y) ∧ ∀x(Student(x) → Reads(x,y))) entails the original formula but the original does not entail it.
chapters.trap: Do not mix the scope of ∀ and ∃: ∀x∃y is not ∃y∀x. Use → with ∀ for restricted quantification, not ∧, or every object in the domain must be a student. Keep free and bound variables straight.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 on levels of language analysis; Unit 3 on syntax trees helps but is not required.
chapters.leave: Parsing algorithms and grammar formalisms belong to Unit 3; theorem proving and full model checking are not examined here.

chapters.idea: Syntax-driven semantic analysis gives every grammar rule a semantic attachment, so the parse tree computes the sentence's logical form compositionally.
chapters.depth: Cover the principle of compositionality and the rule-to-rule hypothesis. Show semantic attachments for lexical rules and for phrase-structure rules: proper names, intransitive and transitive verbs, determiners, NPs, VPs, sentences. Introduce the lambda calculus as the notation for attachments: λx, application, β-reduction, free and bound variables, type checking. Work through quantifier phrases and quantifier scope ambiguity. Explain how attachments ride on a CFG parse and how underspecification can delay quantifier scope. Mention system paradigms only as the pipeline from parser to logical form. Keep semantic features brief; feature-based grammar details are in Unit 3.

figure.title: From parse tree to logical form
figure.aria: A parse tree feeds rule-by-rule semantic attachments, then lambda-reduction produces a logical form that a model can check.

chapters.example: Grammar: S → NP VP; NP → Det N; VP → V NP; NP → Name. Lexical entries: every: λP.λQ.∀x(P(x) → Q(x)); student: λx.Student(x); a: λP.λQ.∃y(P(y) ∧ Q(y)); book: λy.Book(y); reads: λy.λx.Reads(x,y); Ravi: λP.P(Ravi). Build the semantic attachment for 'Every student reads a book' and reduce it to a logical form. Then give the other reading that the same words allow.
chapters.trap: Attach meaning to the rule, not only to words, or composition stops. Apply λ-reduction in the right order and watch λy.λx in a transitive verb. Quantifier scope is not fixed by surface order.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for first-order logic; Unit 3 for CFG rules and parse trees.
chapters.leave: CFG parsing algorithms, feature structures, and grammar coverage to Unit 3; full λ-calculus proofs to a formal semantics course.

chapters.idea: A word form can carry several senses, and those senses are linked by stable relations such as synonymy, antonymy and hyponymy.
chapters.depth: Define lexeme, word form, sense, homonymy, polysemy, synonymy, antonymy (gradable, complementary, reversive), hyponymy and hypernymy, meronymy and holonymy, troponymy for verbs, and the difference between lexical and conceptual relations. Cover sense enumeration and the problem of distinguishing polysemy from homonymy by etymology, relatedness, and the zeugma test. Introduce word similarity using a thesaurus: path length, lowest common subsumer, Wu-Palmer, Resnik and Lin; state each formula and its terms. Use distributional similarity only as a pointer to Unit 5.

figure.aria: A hyponymy tree: dog is a mammal, mammal is an animal, bird is also an animal, and animal is an entity.

chapters.example: For 'bank', give two senses and say whether they are homonyms or polysemous. For 'car', give one synonym, one hypernym, one hyponym, one meronym and one antonym of a related adjective. Then compute the Wu-Palmer similarity between 'dog' and 'cat' if their lowest common subsumer 'carnivore' is at depth 4, 'dog' is at depth 6 and 'cat' is at depth 5.
chapters.trap: Hyponymy has a direction: 'dog' is a hyponym of 'animal'; 'animal' is the hypernym. Homonymy is unrelated senses; polysemy is related senses. A synonym need not fit every context.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 on morphology and word forms; no parsing needed.
chapters.leave: Distributional vectors and embedding similarity to Unit 5; WordNet's full pointer set to Chapter 4.4.

chapters.idea: WordNet and FrameNet turn lexical knowledge into reusable networks: WordNet links word senses by semantic relations, and FrameNet links predicate senses to the roles they take.
chapters.depth: Cover WordNet theory: synset, sense inventory, gloss, lemma, pointer types (hypernym, hyponym, part meronym, antonym, entailment, derivation), the noun hierarchy, sense numbering, and lexicographer files. Show how to read a WordNet entry and how to compute path and Wu-Palmer similarity on the noun graph. Cover FrameNet: frame, frame element (core, peripheral), lexical unit, frame-to-frame relations (inheritance, perspective, subframe), and the difference between a synset and a frame. Describe Indian Language Wordnets and multilingual dictionaries: an IndoWordNet-style synset as an interlingual concept, synset IDs, and the use of a pivot language. Mention metaphor as a short advanced topic: only a few universities teach it; define conceptual metaphor and give one example.

figure.aria: A small WordNet graph: car has hypernyms motor vehicle and vehicle, and hyponyms compact car and used-car.

chapters.example: Using WordNet, write the synset for 'car', give one hypernym and one hyponym, and name the relation between 'car' and 'automobile'. Then name the FrameNet frame for 'buy' and list three core frame elements. Finally, explain how an Indian language wordnet can share the synset 'car' without sharing the word form.
chapters.trap: A synset is a set of synonyms, not one word. Sense numbers are not a frequency guarantee. Frame elements are not WordNet relations and not grammatical relations. Do not treat a multilingual dictionary as a list of exact translations; it links senses.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.3 on word senses and relations.
chapters.leave: WSD algorithms to Chapter 4.5; metaphor processing and full ontology reasoning to advanced courses.

chapters.idea: Word sense disambiguation chooses the sense of a word in context, using a sense inventory, a context window, and either knowledge or a trained classifier.
chapters.depth: State the WSD task and the sense inventory. Cover the most frequent sense baseline. Knowledge-based methods: Lesk, extended Lesk, gloss overlap, graph-based measures over WordNet. Supervised WSD: training data, context features (words in a window, POS, collocations, syntactic features), classifiers (Naive Bayes, decision tree, SVM), and feature selection. Dictionary and thesaurus methods: sense definitions, synonyms, related words. Bootstrapping and semi-supervised methods: seed examples, self-training, co-training, and one-sense-per-discourse. Evaluation: precision, recall, F1, accuracy, Senseval/CoNLL-style test sets, per-sense vs overall. WSD and multilingualism: cross-lingual WSD with parallel corpora and multilingual wordnets; keep this short. Mention distributional similarity but leave vectors to Unit 5.

figure.title: Supervised WSD
figure.aria: A context window becomes a feature vector, a classifier scores the senses, and the highest-scoring sense is chosen.

chapters.example: Disambiguate 'bank' in 'The fisherman sat on the bank of the river.' Use Lesk with two glosses: bank1 'a financial institution that accepts deposits'; bank2 'sloping land beside a river'. Count overlapping words with the context. Then a supervised classifier is tested on four items. The training set has 30 finance senses and 10 river senses; the test set has 2 finance and 2 river items. What is the accuracy of the most frequent sense baseline?
chapters.trap: The most frequent sense baseline is strong; report it. Do not tune on the test set. Lesk can pick the longest gloss by accident, so compare overlaps fairly. A word may keep one sense across a discourse, so context beyond the sentence matters.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.3 and 4.4 for senses and WordNet; Unit 5 for Naive Bayes if the course has covered it.
chapters.leave: Text classification features, TF-IDF and embeddings to Unit 5; full evaluation methodology to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Semantic roles label what each argument does in the event a predicate describes, and selectional restrictions say what kind of filler each slot expects.
chapters.depth: Cover thematic roles: Agent, Patient, Theme, Experiencer, Goal, Source, Instrument, Benefactive, Location, Time. Explain thematic grid, subcategorisation, and diathesis alternations (active/passive, dative, locative). Compare Case Grammar roles with PropBank labels Arg0, Arg1, Arg2 and FrameNet frame elements; state that role inventories differ. Cover selectional restrictions: semantic constraints on arguments, selectional preference and plausibility, violation and coercion, metonymy. Use examples such as 'eat' requiring an animate subject and 'break' requiring a breakable object. Keep the link to lexical semantics explicit: restrictions are stated over word senses.

figure.aria: The predicate broke links to its Agent Ravi, Patient window, Instrument stone and Time yesterday.

chapters.example: Label the semantic roles in 'Ravi broke the window with a stone yesterday in Chennai.' Then state one selectional restriction for the object of 'break' and one for the subject of 'eat'. Say which sentence violates a restriction: 'The stone ate the cake' or 'The child ate the cake'.
chapters.trap: Do not map grammatical subject to Agent automatically: in a passive, the subject is the Patient. Role names vary by theory; use the inventory your syllabus names. Selectional restrictions are preferences with exceptions, not hard grammar rules.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.3 for word senses; Unit 3 for subcategorisation and grammatical relations.
chapters.leave: Full PropBank and FrameNet annotation guidelines to Chapter 4.4 and advanced courses; semantic parsing to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Discourse is coherent when its sentences are linked by relations and cohesive when their surface forms tie together; segmentation finds the units that carry those links.
chapters.depth: Define discourse, utterance, coherence and cohesion. Cover cohesion types from Halliday and Hasan: reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction, lexical cohesion (repetition, synonymy, collocation). Cover coherence relations and Rhetorical Structure Theory: nucleus, satellite, relation names such as Evidence, Result, Cause, Elaboration, Contrast; tree structure and spans. Cover cue phrases and discourse markers, and their ambiguity. Cover discourse segmentation: paragraph and sentence boundaries, cue-phrase-based segmentation, TextTiling and lexical cohesion scores, supervised segmentation. Mention lexical chains. Keep coreference to Chapter 4.8; here pronouns are cohesive devices.

figure.aria: An RST tree with a Result relation: the nucleus Ravi missed the bus is the cause, and the satellite He reached late is the result.

chapters.example: Segment this text into two units and draw an RST tree: 'Ravi missed the bus. As a result, he reached the office late.' Name the coherence relation and list two cohesive devices. Then say whether removing 'As a result' changes the relation.
chapters.trap: Cohesion is not coherence: a text can have pronouns and still be incoherent. RST relations are not sentence-level grammar relations. Cue phrases can be ambiguous ('since' can mark time or cause). A paragraph break is not always a discourse boundary.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for sentence meaning; Chapter 4.6 helps for predicate-argument links.
chapters.leave: Coreference resolution to Chapter 4.8; full RST parsing and corpus annotation to advanced courses.

chapters.idea: Coreference links different mentions to the same entity, and anaphora resolution finds the antecedent that a pronoun or other anaphor depends on.
chapters.depth: Define mention, entity, coreference chain, anaphor, antecedent, cataphora, expletive 'it', and zero anaphora (common in Indian languages). Cover pronoun resolution with Hobbs' algorithm: search the parse tree left-to-right and breadth-first, with number and gender agreement. Cover Centering Theory: discourse entities, forward-looking centres, backward-looking centre, transition types, and how centering constrains pronouns. Cover mention-pair and entity-based models, features (agreement, distance, salience, syntactic role, semantics), and clustering. Cover evaluation: MUC/CoNLL F1 over links or entities; precision, recall, F1. Mention cross-lingual and Indian language issues: dropped pronouns and rich agreement. Keep WSD out except where sense helps.

figure.aria: Three coreference chains: Ravi and He, Meera and She, and report and it.

chapters.example: Resolve the pronouns in: 'Ravi met Meera at the cafe. He was carrying a red folder. Meera asked Ravi for the report. She read it quickly.' Give the coreference chains. Then a system predicts 3 coreference links, of which 2 are correct; the gold standard has 2 links. Compute precision, recall and F1.
chapters.trap: Anaphora is not the same as coreference. Expletive 'it' in 'It is raining' has no antecedent. Do not resolve a pronoun to the nearest noun by default. Evaluate links as the shared task defines them; entity F1 differs from mention F1.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.7 for discourse structure; Chapter 4.6 for semantic roles that help salience; Unit 3 for parse trees for Hobbs.
chapters.leave: Full coreference annotation standards and neural mention-ranking models to Unit 6; WSD to Chapter 4.5.

links: FOL is the target language for semantic attachments

sense relations become the WordNet graph
sense inventory and glosses feed WSD
chosen senses fix predicate argument slots
selectional restrictions are stated over senses
